**Monday, February 29, 1960**

The date itself is the first thing. February 29 occurs only once every four years — roughly one person in 1,461 is born on it — and the calendar withholds it for three years out of four. In 66 years of life, you have had only 16 actual February 29 birthdays. The most recent was in 2024; the next arrives in 2028. Your relationship with your own birthday is, by design of the Gregorian calendar, intermittent. Most people's birthdays come annually, like clockwork. Yours arrives like a comet.

The world that met you on that rare date was in the middle of upheaval.

On the night of February 29, 1960 — at roughly 11:47 PM local time — the Moroccan port city of Agadir was struck by an earthquake. The shaking lasted about fifteen seconds. The old medina collapsed almost completely. When the dust cleared, somewhere between 12,000 and 15,000 people were dead — more than a third of the city's entire population. King Mohammed V flew to the ruins and declared national mourning. Agadir had to be rebuilt from scratch, on new ground, away from the site of the old city entirely. The world you arrived in on February 29, 1960, was simultaneously witnessing one of the worst natural disasters of the decade.

Exactly twenty years before your birth — on **February 29, 1940**, another leap day — Hattie McDaniel became the first African American to win an Academy Award, for her role in *Gone with the Wind*. She was escorted to a segregated table at the back of the ballroom, separated from the white cast members and the assembled Hollywood elite. She won anyway. She gave a gracious speech and she wept. The people who made her sit at that back table were certain they were enforcing a permanent social order. Twenty years later, the child born on the next February 29 arrived into a world that was beginning — painfully, violently, against fierce resistance — to prove them wrong.

**Twenty-eight days before you were born** — on February 1, 1960 — four Black college students sat at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, ordered coffee, and were refused service. They did not leave. By the time you arrived on February 29, the sit-in movement had already spread to dozens of cities across the South. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee would be founded that April. The Civil Rights Movement was no longer building toward a confrontation; it had arrived. The child born on the last day of February 1960 entered a country in the act of reckoning with itself.

1960 was a hinge year in a broader sense. Seventeen African nations gained independence that year — historians call it the Year of Africa — as the European colonial order, already cracking since Suez, came apart with startling speed. It was the year Kennedy and Nixon held the first televised presidential debates, demonstrating for the first time that television would determine politics. It was the year the U-2 spy plane piloted by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union, blowing up the Paris summit and making clear that the Cold War's surveillance dimensions reached into the stratosphere. The world of 1960 was reorganizing itself under new pressures, at new speeds, and no one could fully see where it was going.

You were born three years after Sputnik, one year before Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth. The Space Age had already begun. It had simply not yet sent anyone to the Moon. You grew up in the decade that did.

Consider the full arc. You arrived when the world held roughly 3 billion people; it now holds more than 8 billion. In 66 years you have watched: the Kennedy assassination (age 3); the Moon landing (age 9); Nixon's resignation (age 14); the personal computer revolution through your twenties; the fall of the Berlin Wall (age 29); the collapse of the Soviet Union (age 31); the internet remaking everyday life through your thirties and forties; 9/11 (age 41); the smartphone (age 47); a global pandemic (age 60); and now, at 66, an AI revolution that is changing what it means to write, to know things, and to think.

You were born on a day the calendar barely admits exists, into a morning already carrying news of disaster, and into a nation whose best reckoning with itself was just underway. The world of February 29, 1960, was not stable — it was a world actively in the process of becoming something else. In 66 years, you have watched it become several something elses since, each more surprising than the last. And on that rarest of dates, you will be back for another one in 2028.
